steps.title: Smell starts with a breath
steps.text: A cup of coffee gives off odorant molecules. Everything you smell arrives with the air you breathe in through your nose.

steps.title: Only what smelling needs
steps.text: The airway, the olfactory nerve and the brain areas it reaches. Everything else fades away.

steps.title: 1 · Sniff
steps.text: He lifts the coffee to his nose. Inhaled air passes a small patch high in the nasal cavity, the olfactory epithelium; most of it goes on down the throat. A sniff sends more air up to the patch.
quotes: As airborne molecules are inhaled through the nose, they pass over the olfactory epithelial region

steps.title: 2 · Odorants meet receptors
steps.text: Under the roof of the nose. Odorants dissolve in the mucus and reach the neurons' cilia. Each neuron has one receptor type (about 350 in humans); each odorant fits several, so a smell is a combination.
quotes: Some receptors detect more than one odor

steps.title: 3 · Through the skull
steps.text: Cut open from the side. The neurons' axons bundle into the olfactory nerve and pass through tiny holes in the cribriform plate, the roof of the ethmoid bone, to the olfactory bulb above.
quotes: through an olfactory foramen in the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone

steps.title: 4 · Olfactory bulb: sorting by receptor
steps.text: Zoomed in at the plate. All neurons of one receptor type (colour) send their axons to the same glomerulus; mitral cells carry it on along the tract. A smell becomes a pattern of active glomeruli.
quotes: each glomerulus receives signals from one type of olfactory receptor

steps.title: But how do we see this?
steps.text: Back down through the plate, out of the nose, and there he is: the coffee drinker has been wearing a VR headset all along. So how do we see these 3D scenes, and how were they made?

steps.title: From 3D models to files the headset can draw
steps.text: Four models went in. The raw files are big and full of things a real-time scene doesn't need, so we kept only the parts we show and made them lighter, ending as four small .glb files.

steps.title: Loaded by three.js
steps.text: three.js, the 3D library our page uses, has many arms. The GLTFLoader arm grabs the four files and reads them into meshes; the WebGL arm pushes them into the GPU's memory, once.

steps.title: Every frame
steps.text: Then on every frame: the head pose comes up through OpenXR and WebXR, three.js updates the scene, the GPU draws it twice (one view per eye), and the frame goes back down through them to the displays. Slowed down here: really 72 to 120 times a second.

steps.title: One road to the headset: OpenXR
steps.text: Our page isn't the only way in. three.js is to us what Unity or Unreal is to a game, and WebXR, inside the browser, does the job of their OpenXR plug-in. Underneath, all of them use the same layer, OpenXR: one standard way to talk to a headset. Each one waits for the next frame, gets the head pose, and hands back the picture it drew.
quotes: OpenXR is a royalty-free, open standard that provides a common set of APIs for developing XR applications

steps.title: How every scene is built
steps.text: That's the road out. Our side of it: each scene is a folder of the same shape, code in sequence.js, words in steps.json, models in .glb files. One page plays them in turn, in one VR session, and every scene plugs into it the same way. The library is three.js, which reaches the headset through WebXR. This part, the Presentation, lives inside Smelling's folder.

steps.title: All inside our website
steps.text: Everything you have seen, the man, the anatomy, these boards, is one web page, opened in the headset's browser.
